title: Cleo and the Charm of Joy
markdown:
Cleo loved Whispering Hill. Every morning she zipped her bright blue overalls, took her sturdy bicycle, and carried parcels to the cozy houses along the winding roads. Each package was a small promise, and she liked those promises neat, clean, and on time. The breeze through the pines agreed with her. She smoothed the overalls, checked the saddlebag buckles, and breathed. This was her orderly world, and she meant to keep it.

Today the world had other plans.

The first oddness was Mrs. Gable’s knitting box. It usually balanced on a finger, all soft yarn and no secrets. Today it sat in the bag like a box of polished stones. Cleo lifted it, set it down, lifted it again. Still heavy. She checked the label twice, as if a wrong name could add ounces.

Then came Mr. Fitzwilliam’s bird feeder, a cheerful wooden thing that ought to have ridden lightly. It strained the handlebars as if it had been poured from lead. The bicycle complained up the first hill. Unease ran down Cleo’s spine, not cold, just wrong. Deliveries were supposed to behave. A grumpy cloud had sat on her sunny route, and she did not know its name. She thought of her log, the neat ticks, the way Whispering Hill trusted her not to be late. That trust suddenly felt like another weight.

“Something’s not right, Vex,” she told the empty air.

A faint shiver passed her shoulder: Vex, the parcel poltergeist, her quiet invisible companion. He could feel the extra something in the packages, a thrum. His nudges usually made things wobble, which Cleo liked about as much as spilled string.

“The parcels feel fizzy,” said his voice in her mind, like a forgotten sweet wrapper. “As if they’ve swallowed a tiny cloud. Or a flock of them.”

She set her jaw. “We need to find the weight. If we don’t, Mrs. Gable’s scarf waits, and Mr. Fitzwilliam’s birds go hungry.” Neighbours without yarn, birds without seed: a clock she could hear without looking.

Their search took them to the dusty attic of the old delivery depot, a place Cleo usually left to spiders. Old paper, dried lavender, forgotten corners. Cobwebs hung like grey beards. Dust motes used the thin light for a dance. A rustle in a shadowy stack made her jump; her hands clenched the handlebars. Mess, or worse. Vex flinched too, invisibility wavering like heat. In his startle he bumped a tower of boxes. Thump-crash-rattle. Disorder, loud. The tidy route called like a blanket. She almost turned back.

“Careful,” she whispered, tight. “Quiet. No more mess.”

“Sorry.” He sounded like wind in dry leaves. “This place is full of old secrets. Some of them jump.”

They pressed on, his faint shimmer a thread through gloom. Among forgotten ribbons, faded bows, and a stuffed owl wearing a century of dust, they found it: a tiny shimmering charm, a fallen star gone dim and sad, pulsing forlorn. It added a little shadow-weight to whatever it touched.

“A wrapping charm,” Vex said, a sigh in the words. “They’re meant to make people gasp when they open a gift. A bit of extra wonder. No one has been happy enough lately to keep them bright. They feel forgotten.”

The charm wanted work. It had been left at the bottom of the world’s toy box. Cleo saw that helping it would mean loosening her perfect system: letting Vex be Vex, wobble and all. She hesitated. The schedule was her pride. The charm’s faint pulse was a sad sound in the quiet. Loneliness can be as heavy as stones in a knitting box.

“All right,” she said, shaky and firm. “We’ll help it shine.”

The charm was warm on her fingertips, and heavy with being unseen. She let Vex take it, invisible hands gentler than his attic manners. Going down, dust clung. His slightly clumsy hover was a reminder she had let go of the balloon. She did not snatch it back.

On the hill they set the charm on a small velvet cushion on the cart, where sun could find it. Cleo began her rounds the long way, past the pine bend and the house with the blue gate, because the charm seemed to like the light. Vex, with a giggle like tinkling bells, nudged the sunflower bouquet meant for old Mr. Henderson. A speck of warm light settled on the yellow heads and stayed there, polite as a bee.

Mr. Henderson came out wiping his hands on a tea towel. When Cleo handed the flowers over, he did not merely smile. He gasped. His eyes went bright as water in noon.

“These are wonderful. They feel so cheerful. I had forgotten sunflowers could do that.”

Warmth spread through Cleo, better than a ticked list. Behind her, the cart gave a tiny wobble. She let it.

Mrs. Gable’s yarn, when it finally arrived, seemed no heavier than yarn should be. Mrs. Gable held up a skein to the window and said it looked like it wanted to be a scarf already. Mr. Fitzwilliam’s feeder went up on its hook without straining anyone’s arms; a tit landed before he had stepped back, as if it had been waiting for permission.

After that the deliveries were a little less predictable and a little more themselves. A package might wobble. A ribbon might keep an extra sparkle. Whispering Hill gasped more often, in the good way. The tight knot in Cleo’s middle loosened into something like looking forward.

At young Lily’s gate she handed over a bright red ribbon around a small box of cookies. A faint warm light, cousin to the charm, settled on Lily’s nose. Cleo did not flinch, did not fuss, did not open the log. She smiled a true smile, the bicycle ticking in the pine air, and left the imperfect joy to finish the delivery on its own. Vex brushed her shoulder, a thank-you with no wrapper, and the charm on its cushion kept a steady, ordinary shine, the kind a parcel can carry without anyone having to announce it.
